input_signals.name: Double Confirmation Value Payout
input_signals.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Mispricing is revealed only when the price-based and management-based valuation signals agree: firms that are simultaneously in the cheap tail and the net-repurchase tail are genuinely undervalued, firms simultaneously in the expensive tail and the net-issuance tail are genuinely overvalued, and firms where the two disagree (cheap issuers, expensive repurchasers) carry no reliable information and should be pushed to the middle of the distribution.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the additive SUMRANK with a conjunctive MIN of ranks makes the score a true AND-operator: the "both good" term only rises when the weaker of the two dimensions rises, and subtracting the symmetric "both bad" conjunction builds the short leg from expensive issuers rather than from any firm with a low sum. Because disagreement cases collapse to a neutral score, the long-short spread is by construction an interaction portfolio and cannot be replicated by any weighted average of book-to-market and payout yield.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( min( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), min( rank( neg( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Book Equity Retired Per Market Dollar
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MUL(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ceq), MUL(MUL(prcc_f, csho), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The per-share value created by a buyback equals the dollars spent times the discount at which shares are retired, so a dollar of repurchase transfers far more book value to remaining holders when price-to-book is low; symmetrically, a firm that sells equity below book destroys per-share value and is signalling financing desperation rather than opportunistic timing.
input_signals.reasoning: This is an inherently multiplicative quantity — net repurchase yield scaled by the inverse of the market-to-book multiple — so it cannot be decomposed into the value and payout anomalies acting separately, and it replaces the earlier noisy binary SIGN moderator with a continuous, economically interpretable intensity. The long tail is cheap aggressive repurchasers and the short tail is cheap aggressive issuers, which is the value-destruction case the accretion arithmetic actually identifies, not the sign-flip artifact the critic correctly rejected.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( mul( sub( prstkc, sstk ), ceq ), mul( mul( prcc_f, csho ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Self Funded Payout At Cheap Enterprise Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters is not payout itself but its funding source: cheap enterprises returning capital out of internally generated cash while also retiring debt are shrinking total claims from strength, whereas cheap enterprises whose payout is financed by new borrowing, or which must raise net external capital, are levering into a discount and are value traps.
input_signals.reasoning: The valuation leg now enters as a non-negative rank multiplier on the signed capital-return flow, so the signal is a genuine conditional statement — capital-return intensity is priced only where the enterprise is cheap on EBITDA/EV — rather than the additive rank blend the critic flagged. Both numerator and denominator of the financing leg are now measured at enterprise value, fixing the inconsistent equity-market-cap scaling, and subtracting net debt issuance strips out debt-funded buybacks that mimic the signal without any real contraction of claims.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Contrarian Buyback At Own Valuation Low
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Managerial conviction is most informative when it is contrarian relative to the firm's own valuation history: buying back stock when the firm trades at the cheap end of its own five-year book-to-market range reveals private information that the decline is unwarranted, whereas issuing equity precisely at the firm's own valuation trough reveals a binding financing constraint.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the horizon-smoothing tweak the critic rejected and replaces the cross-sectional value dimension with a within-firm, time-series valuation position, so the signal identifies a timing decision rather than re-sorting on the level of book-to-market or composite issuance. Because TS_RANK is firm-relative it is orthogonal to the size and style tilts that drive standard value-plus-buyback composites, and the multiplicative form means firms at their own valuation highs receive near-zero scores regardless of payout.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 5 ), winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Rich Valuation Equity Issuance Intensity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(RATIO(sstk, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Equity issuance predicts poor returns mainly because managers time it to windows of overvaluation, so the same dollar of stock sold is far more bearish when the firm trades at a high market-to-book multiple; issuance by low-multiple firms is closer to genuine financing need and carries much weaker negative information.
input_signals.reasoning: The direction is now internally consistent: the non-negative expensiveness rank amplifies issuance intensity, so richly valued heavy issuers earn the highest scores and the EXPECTED_SIGN is negative, placing them in the short leg exactly as the market-timing story requires. Replacing raw csho growth with cash-flow-statement equity sales scaled by market capitalization eliminates the split and stock-dividend contamination the critic identified while keeping a continuous, well-populated distribution.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), winsor( ratio( sstk, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Yield Conditional Deleveraging
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A high operating cash-flow yield is a discount only if the firm is not consuming that cash to service an expanding debt load; cheap, cash-generative firms that are repaying long-term debt are deleveraging toward a re-rating, while cheap, cash-generative firms simultaneously raising net new debt are distress-financed and their apparent yield reflects credit risk rather than mispricing.
input_signals.reasoning: The structure is now multiplicative rather than an additive pairing of cash-flow-to-price with Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan external financing, and the financing leg is restricted to the long-term debt channel so it does not duplicate the equity-issuance signals elsewhere in the batch. Conditioning concentrates the bet inside the high-cash-yield group, where the value-trap versus true-discount distinction is economically live, while expensive firms receive scores near zero and stay out of both legs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), neg( winsor( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry Relative Cheap Self Funded Payout
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Enterprise multiples are set at the industry level, so a firm cheap relative to its own industry peers while returning capital funded internally rather than by new borrowing is mispriced, whereas the raw cross-sectional EV multiple mostly ranks industries and therefore reproduces a static value tilt.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates one specific design choice against the best generation-0 result (fmb 3.90, alpha +0.010): swapping the cross-sectional rank for an industry rank in the valuation moderator, holding the internally-funded capital-return leg fixed. If the industry-neutral version raises the FF5 alpha while keeping the slope, it confirms that the missing alpha was an industry/value-tilt artifact rather than a defect of the payout-funding mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Net Cash Valuation Repurchase
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: When a large fraction of market capitalization is covered by net cash on the balance sheet, the operating business is being valued at almost nothing; management repurchasing shares in that state is converting excess liquidity into the cheapest asset it can buy, while a firm in the same state issuing equity signals that the cash is committed or the business is impaired.
input_signals.reasoning: Net cash to price is a valuation metric that HML (book-to-market) spans poorly because book equity mixes cash with operating assets, so the value tilt that absorbed prior alphas should be much weaker here. The interaction is economically necessary: high net cash alone is a known low-return "cash trap" characteristic, and it only becomes bullish when management demonstrably deploys the cash into its own undervalued equity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( che, add( dltt, dlc ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap Equity For Debt Swap
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(MIN(RATIO(SUB(dltis, dltr), at), RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: When managers believe their equity is cheap relative to their debt, the value-maximizing action is a capital-structure swap — raise long-term debt and retire shares — so a cheap firm doing both simultaneously is making a costly, leverage-increasing bet on its own stock, while a cheap firm doing the reverse swap (selling equity to repay debt) is deleveraging under duress and confirms the discount is warranted.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is no longer a net payout yield, so this is not a rescaling of book-equity-retired-per-market-dollar: the MIN operator requires both debt issuance and equity retirement to be positive, isolating genuine recapitalizations from ordinary cash-funded buybacks and from debt raised to fund capex. Direction is now internally coherent — the non-negative cheapness rank means overvalued issuers sit near zero rather than in the long leg — and the signal deliberately contrasts with the accepted self-funded-payout proposal, so the batch tells us whether the funding source of a buyback helps or hurts.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), winsor( min( ratio( sub( dltis, dltr ), at ), ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Unlevered Cheap Repurchaser
input_signals.expression: MUL(MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness means mispricing only when the firm has the balance-sheet slack to act on it: a low-leverage firm trading at a high book-to-market that retires equity is buying a discount it can afford, whereas an equally cheap but heavily indebted firm is priced for leverage risk and its financing choices are dictated by creditors rather than by managerial valuation opinion.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops all past-return and valuation-change conditioning, so it is not a horizon variant of the contrarian-buyback signal; the new conditioning axis is the leverage state, a financing-theme variable that separates distressed value from mispriced value. Because the MIN conjunction damps highly levered deep-value names — exactly the firms whose returns FF5's HML and CMA loadings already explain — the surviving spread should be less factor-spanned and more likely to show abnormal return rather than a repackaged value tilt.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( min( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), at ) ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Industry Neutral Both Legs Capital Return
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Payout and issuance norms are as industry-specific as valuation multiples — utilities and banks systematically pay out, biotech and tech systematically issue — so the informative part of a firm's capital-return decision is its deviation from peer practice, and pairing that deviation with industry-relative cheapness should isolate firm-specific managerial conviction.
input_signals.reasoning: Industry-ranking only the valuation leg already lifted alpha from 0.010 to 0.014 and Sharpe from 0.35 to 0.42, so the natural next question is whether the residual factor exposure sits in the financing leg's industry composition. IND_ADJ demeans the capital-return intensity within industry while preserving its sign and magnitude, which keeps the economic content intact and removes the sector bets that likely load on CMA and RMW.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( ind_adj( ratio( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Conversion Enterprise Yield Capital Return
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: EBITDA overstates distributable cash for firms with heavy working-capital absorption or non-cash revenue, so measuring enterprise cheapness with realized operating cash flow should identify firms whose capital return is genuinely fundable and screen out accrual-inflated cheap multiples.
input_signals.reasoning: The financing leg is held fixed against the archive's best signal so the comparison isolates the quality of the valuation numerator, which matters because the mechanism claims the payout is internally funded — a claim EBITDA cannot verify but oancf can. If cash-flow yield strengthens both the slope and the alpha, it tells us the interaction is really about funded conviction rather than about the accounting multiple.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( oancf, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Sustained Claim Contraction At Cheap Enterprise Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(TS_SUM(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), 3), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year of self-funded capital return can be a one-off recapitalization or an asset-sale artifact, whereas three consecutive years of shrinking total claims while trading cheap identifies a management team with a standing policy of buying its own undervalued capital, which should be both more persistent and more slowly priced by the market.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a horizon ablation of the winning family, justified by evidence rather than by novelty: the one-year version's alpha (0.014, t 1.42) is economically meaningful but imprecise, and if the imprecision comes from year-to-year lumpiness in repurchase and debt flows, cumulating three years of the same construct should raise ls_talpha and Sharpe without changing the economic story. If instead the alpha falls, we learn the signal is news-driven, which would redirect the search toward the change-based designs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( ratio( ts_sum( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), 3 ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Financing Direction Purity At Cheap Book Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), ADD(ADD(prstkc, sstk), dvt)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: The credibility of a financing signal lies in its direction relative to total capital-market activity, not its dollar size: a cheap firm whose entire gross activity is share retirement, with no offsetting issuance, is making an unambiguous valuation statement, whereas a cheap firm churning stock in both directions is running option programs rather than expressing conviction.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the payout-composition signal that produced alpha 0.021 with a null slope: normalizing by gross activity (prstkc + sstk + dvt) makes the measure bounded and scale-free, so it is no longer dominated by repurchase intensity and no longer inherits the size and investment-factor loadings that flatten yield-based versions. Because the moderator is a bounded direction score rather than a yield, the resulting spread should be much less collinear with CMA, giving the interaction a cleaner chance at FF5 alpha and a nonzero cross-sectional slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), add( add( prstkc, sstk ), dvt ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Own Equity Versus Real Investment Choice
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), GROWTH(at, 1)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Every financing decision is a revealed-preference statement about the firm's opportunity set: when a cheaply valued enterprise chooses to retire its own shares while holding or shrinking its asset base, management is stating that its own equity is a better investment than any project it could fund, whereas a cheaply valued firm simultaneously expanding assets and selling stock is stating the opposite and is usually diluting shareholders into low-return growth.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a new hypothesis rather than a one-term deletion — the financing leg is now a *contrast* between two competing uses of capital (share retirement versus asset expansion) instead of a payout yield, so it cannot collapse to the published shareholder-yield anomaly crossed with value. The interaction is economically necessary because the same allocation choice carries opposite information at rich valuations, and because the differenced construction nets out the common scale of the firm's financing activity, it should carry less mechanical CMA loading than either component alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( sub( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), at ), growth( at, 1 ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Within Cheap Capital Return Conditional
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), 0.7), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Among firms the market already prices as cheap on enterprise cash earnings, the financing decision is the variable that separates genuine mispricing from justified discount: cheap firms retiring claims out of internal cash are undervalued, cheap firms raising net external capital are impaired, and this comparison should hold with no help from the value premium itself.
input_signals.reasoning: The hard indicator switches the financing signal on only inside the cheapest 30% of the cross-section, so both the long and short legs are drawn from the same valuation stratum and the HML/CMA loadings that absorbed 3 percentage points of raw return in the archive's best signal should largely cancel. This is a structural fix for the diagnosed absorption problem rather than a new characteristic, and it makes the surviving spread interpretable as the pure within-value financing effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), 0.7 ), winsor( ratio( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Within Expensive Net Issuance Conditional
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.7), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Overvaluation is only actionable when management acts on it: within the richly valued 30% of the market, the firms selling stock are cashing in on the premium and should underperform the otherwise identical rich firms that are buying stock back, so the issuance effect exists conditional on high valuation and not merely as a proxy for being a growth stock.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's rich-valuation issuance signal produced a wrong-signed FF5 alpha (+0.048) precisely because its long and short legs straddled the valuation spectrum, handing FF5 enormous negative HML/RMW loadings to price; restricting both legs to expensive firms removes that gradient. This is the short-side counterpart to Signal 1 and, evaluated alongside it, tells us whether the interaction's abnormal return lives in the undervalued corner, the overvalued corner, or both.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( ratio( mul( prcc_f, csho ), ceq ) ), 0.7 ), winsor( ratio( sub( sstk, prstkc ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Drawdown Repurchase Conviction
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(prcc_f, TS_MAX(prcc_f, 5)))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Managers know their own reservation price better than any accounting ratio conveys: buying back stock when the price sits far below its own five-year peak is a direct statement that the drawdown is unwarranted, whereas selling equity into the same drawdown signals that the decline reflects real deterioration and a binding need for cash.
input_signals.reasoning: The conditioning variable is a pure price-history state with no accounting input, so unlike book-to-market it is not spanned by HML — and FF5 contains no momentum or drawdown factor at all, which is where the alpha in this family has repeatedly leaked away. It differs from the archive's contrarian-buyback signal because that used the time-series rank of book-to-market, which is contaminated by book-equity growth and is a much noisier proxy for distance from peak valuation.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( prcc_f, ts_max( prcc_f, 5 ) ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( prstkc, sstk ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Non Liquidating Cheap Capital Return
input_signals.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)), 0.3), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The capital-return signal means something different in a shrinking business than in a stable one: among firms that are not liquidating their asset base, returning capital out of internal cash is a statement of surplus earnings power, whereas the same statistic in a contracting firm is simply asset runoff that the investment factor already prices.
input_signals.reasoning: Growth now enters as a sample restriction rather than a multiplicative amplifier, so both legs are drawn from the same non-shrinking population — the short leg is a non-liquidating cheap firm raising external capital, not a fast-growing issuer, which removes the asset-growth-anomaly restatement the critic identified. Excluding only the bottom 30% of asset growth keeps roughly seventy percent of firms eligible, so portfolio composition stays broad and stable rather than concentrating in a rare triple-condition corner.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( indicator( rank( growth( at, 1 ) ), 0.3 ), mul( ind_rank( ratio( ebitda, add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ) ), winsor( ratio( sub( sub( add( prstkc, dvc ), sstk ), sub( dltis, dltr ) ), add( sub( add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), dltt ), che ), dlc ) ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Stability Weighted Cheap Capital Return
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltis, sstk), ADD(dltr, prstkc)), at), 5))), MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ADD(prstkc, dvc), sstk), SUB(dltis, dltr)), ADD(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), dltt), che), dlc)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A financing decision is credible evidence about valuation only when it reflects deliberate policy rather than external circumstance, so the current capital-return choice of a cheap firm should be weighted by how stable that firm's external financing has been: steady self-funders are making a judgment, while firms whose capital-market activity lurches year to year are being pushed around by lenders and markets.
input_signals.reasoning: The sign inconsistency is fixed — stability now enters as a nonnegative rank weight multiplying the *signed* capital-return flow, so the long leg is cheap, stable, capital-returning firms and the short leg is cheap, stable, capital-raising firms, with erratic financiers damped toward zero instead of dominating either tail. Measuring volatility on an asset-scaled flow ratio rather than on dollar amounts removes the mechanical size confound, and the weight is a cross-sectional rank so general firm-level volatility enters only through its ordering, not its level.
